newsitem.title: USA: U.S. property insurers' loss reserves down -- report.
newsitem.headline: U.S. property insurers' loss reserves down -- report.

text.p: The U.S. property-casualty insurance industry's core loss reserves began to materially weaken in 1996, reversing several years of favorable reserve trends, rating agency A.M. Best said in a report released this week.

A.M. Best's proprietary loss reserve model shows that the industry's carried core reserves -- all reserves except those maintained to cover asbestos and environmental -- will be about $35 billion, or 10 percent, below Best's estimate of ultimate required reserves at year-end 1996.

This would represent a $5 billion deterioration from 1995 that reflects continued harvesting of prior-year reserve redundancies and lower reserve margins being booked in the current accident year, A.M. Best said.
The deficiency increases to 23 percent after fully incorporating A.M. Best's $51 billion estimate of the industry's unfunded asbestos and environmental liabilities.
Annual growth in loss reserves has slowed from a high of nearly 20 percent in the mid-1980s to roughly 2.5 percent in 1996, the A.M. Best said.
This slowdown is consistent with reduced loss cost trends in the industry's dominant personal auto and workers' compensation lines in recent years.
However, an increasingly poor pricing environment and flattening investment earnings also are contributing to the decline in the rate of loss-reserve growth and growing loss-reserve inadequacies.

Commercial carriers face mounting profit-margin pressures and eroding rates, principally within the workers' compensation, general/products liability, commercial auto, commercial package and medical malpractice lines.
Collectively, these lines constitute the majority of the property-casualty industry's total loss reserves.

A.M. Best said this decline in core reserves does not bode well for the industry, particularly in light of the deterioration of premium adequacy in most commercial lines over the past 12 months, ongoing asbestos and environmental liabilities and uncertainty presented by mass tort liabilities.
Loss-reserve adequacy is critical to insurers' ratings, A.M. Best said.

"Widening reserve adequacy gaps among insurers will further differentiate stronger companies from weaker ones that might otherwise appear to maintain comparable financial strength," the A.M. Best report said.
While industrywide trends are not yet alarming, A.M. Best said the disparity between individual insurers' reserve adequacy levels is growing.

A.M. Best said it is most concerned about carriers that exhibit unstable loss-reserve trends, that have established unrealistically low current accident-year loss ratios and that exhibit aggressive growth in competitively priced, commodity-driven segments.
As a result, the rating agency said it continues to sharpen its focus on all aspects of price and loss reserve adequacy and to downgrade insurers that do not maintain adequate reserves.
